newsitem.title: USA: Dollar rises to 6-year high vs. mark on upbeat Fed view.
newsitem.headline: Dollar rises to 6-year high vs. mark on upbeat Fed view.

text.p: The dollar rose to a fresh six-year high against the German mark on Wednesday, extending a powerful rally in the wake of Tuesday's upbeat assessment of the U.S. economy by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.
But the advance lost some steam after Fed Vice Chair Alice Rivlin said the dollar may not get much stronger.

The dollar jumped in early trading, topping 1.83 marks for the first time since August 1991. Overseas investors flocked to the dollar, attracted by buoyant U.S. financial markets after Greenspan delivered the first part of his two-day congressional testimony on the economy.

"The overnight markets tended to focus more on the fact that bonds and stocks in the U.S. rallied on the remarks, and that the U.S. economy is the best of all possible worlds -- sustainable growth and low inflation," said David Gilmore, at Foreign Exchange Analytics, a Connecticut consulting firm.
The dollar ended at 1.8250 marks, up from 1.8245 marks on Tuesday. It rose to 115.68 yen from 115.00 yen.

U.S. markets calmed a bit on Wednesday, providing less support for the dollar than the previous session, when the Dow Jones industrial average jumped nearly 155 points and bond yields, which move in the opposite direction from prices, fell to their lowest level in almost eight months.
The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell slightly Wednesday and the Dow gained about 27 points to 8,088.

Greenspan continued his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony before the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday. But his address had little impact on trading, being mostly a rehash of the previous day's remarks to the House banking committee.
Traders were unsure how to interpret Rivlin's remarks, which could have also been construed as an endorsement of a strong dollar.

Rivlin told legislators Wednesday that the strength of the dollar had helped to keep import prices in check, and thus curb overall inflation, but that the currency was unlikely to race ahead much further.
"I'm not sure that what she said was considered new information from her," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange trading manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan.
"Keep in mind that dollar commentary is not in the Fed's purview, anyway," Pettit added.
In other trading, the dollar rose to 1.4845 Swiss francs from 1.4825 on Tuesday and to Canadian $1.3820 from C$1.3782.
